Harley Reid: West Coast's best and fairest winner went up to 78 a game in his third year, attending 80% of centre bounces and topping out at 136. Fantasy-wise the polish isn't there yet: 67% disposal efficiency and plenty of contested chaos keep him short of the elite. A shoulder clean-up is done, but a two-match ban for a dangerous tackle means coaches start 2027 without him.
Mitch Georgiades: Seven seasons in, Georgiades has lifted his average every year he's had a decent run, landing at 72 off 2.4 goals and four marks inside 50 a game. That's about as good as a pure key forward gets in this format, with no midfield minutes to fall back on. Think reliable forward-line depth, not a match-winner.
Joel Freijah: Three years at the Dogs, three steps up: 62, 71, now 76 over a full 25 games. Freijah does a bit of everything on the wing and through the middle (38% CBA), and that MID/FWD tag is handy. A 104 in round 24 suggests he finished the year with something left.
Bodhi Uwland: No regular on this list made a bigger jump in 2026. Uwland went from 63 to 87 once the Suns handed him the kick-ins (106 of them), and he used the ball at 85% while picking off 6.5 intercepts a game. At 23, that role turns him from a bench defender into a weekly starter.
Harry McKay: The 2021 Coleman medallist had his best fantasy years in 2024 and 2025, hovering around 80, before slipping to 67 in 2026 despite playing 23 games. His scores swung from 40 to 116 in the last five alone, and only 1.5 goals a game won't carry him. At 29, he's a forward you start on form, not by default.
George Wardlaw: There's real hunger in Wardlaw's game, with 5.4 tackles and 60% of centre bounces, but he's on the ground only 61% of the time. That's why his 0.95 points per minute turns into a modest 71.5. Find him more minutes and the scoring follows; until then he's a 70s midfielder who missed the last two rounds.
Harry Morrison: Morrison is a half-back and wing type who gets to 72 on uncontested ball and intercepts, with zero centre bounce work. Consistency is the issue: a 35 and a 105 sat inside his final five games. Fifteen games in 2026 continues a career of patchy availability, so he's a useful fill-in at best.
Will Day: When Day plays, he scores: 0.93 points per minute in 2026 and a 95-point season back in 2023. He just doesn't play enough, managing 35 games across the last three years. Hawthorn are using him through the middle at 57% CBA, so a clean run would pay off handsomely, but keeping him means betting on his body.
Finn O'Sullivan: A 20-year-old attending 68% of centre bounces is not normal. O'Sullivan jumped from 54 to 72 in his second season at North, and the DEF/MID eligibility gives coaches a midfielder's role in a defender's slot. He's one of the better long-term keeper holds in this group.
Charlie Curnow: Curnow is a goals-or-bust forward: 3.1 a game in his second year as a Swan, no centre bounce work and barely two handballs. That brings a 130 one week and a 49 the next, as his last five showed. His 82.7 in 2023 looks like the peak now, and at 30 he's a matchup play rather than a lock.
Oliver Francou: Francou only got four games into his debut season with the Eagles, but they were promising ones: 74.8 a game with six tackles and nearly nine contested possessions. He finished the year flagged with a season-ending injury, so 2027 is basically a fresh start. Small sample, intriguing upside.
Nick Watson: Hawthorn's 170cm crowd favourite bounced back from a 49.5 slump to 68 in 2026, kicking 2.7 goals a game. Small forwards rarely build big fantasy averages, and Watson's scores swing hard with his kicking (a 90 followed straight away by a 29 late in the year). Fun to own, frustrating to rely on.
Mac Andrew: At 202cm, Andrew plays as Gold Coast's intercepting tall: 7.1 intercepts a game, 84% disposal efficiency and 91% time on ground. That lifted him to 72, a career best, but key defenders without kick-ins hit a fantasy ceiling, and Uwland has the ones that matter. A steady D5 more than anything.
Brayden Maynard: Two hundred and forty-six games into his career, Maynard posted his best average since 2021 (78.6) on the back of four rebound 50s a game and a share of the kick-ins. The concern is the off-season: a shoulder reconstruction means he won't train fully until the new year. Expect a slow start before he gets going.
Ryan Maric: Maric's 2025 breakout to 75 suggested West Coast had found something in a 196cm utility. Then 2026 brought only 12 games at 65, with a top score of 84. The DEF/MID eligibility is useful, but he needs to show the 2025 version was real before anyone pays for him.
Josh Worrell: Adelaide's kick-in man has crept up every season: 69, 77, now 79 across 24 games, built on 75 kick-ins, 5.5 rebound 50s and 84% efficiency. His late season was patchy (41 and 59 in the run home), so the scores are steady rather than spectacular. His July driving case ended in a fine with no ban reported, so his availability isn't affected.
Nick Bryan: Thirteen games was a career-high for Bryan, which tells you most of his story: 36 games in six seasons. When he plays he's Essendon's number one ruck (72% CBA, 24 hitouts), but 62 a game is pedestrian for that role. He's a keeper stash on the hope that the body finally holds up.
Nathan O'Driscoll: O'Driscoll leaves Fremantle for Richmond after a 2026 spent mostly off half-back and on the wing, attending just 3% of centre bounces. The Tigers' midfield offers more opportunity, which is the whole appeal at 64 a game. He faded badly late, though, posting 49, 38 and 42 to finish the year.
Aaron Cadman: The 2022 number one pick is becoming a footballer, but not yet a fantasy one. Cadman has gone 25, 46, 59, 61, with 1.8 goals a game, and his 0.53 points per minute is poor for someone on the ground 91% of the time. Keep him for what he might become, not for points now.
Harry Dean: Twenty-two games as a 19-year-old key defender is a strong first year at Carlton, and his 5.2 intercepts show where the game is headed. The fantasy output is still only 50 a game, with no kick-ins and few disposals. A development hold who could be worth more in two years.
Josh Weddle: Weddle has been stuck between 58 and 70 for four seasons now, and 2026 drifted back to 65 with a best of 94. He's a dashing half-back for Hawthorn, but without kick-ins or midfield time the numbers stay flat. The DEF/MID tag is his main selling point.
Darcy Fort: Brisbane needed Fort in all 26 games, but his fantasy average fell from 73 to 58. He's playing 60% of game time, splitting the ruck with 15 hitouts, and has hit 82 at best. At 33, the 2025 numbers look like the high point.
Sam Cumming: Fourteen games into his first season at Richmond, Cumming averaged 58.6 with 43% of centre bounces, a decent sign for a teenager. A 72 in round 20 was his last full game before a 25 and a season-ending injury. Plenty of keeper upside if he's right for pre-season.
Cooper Duff-Tytler: The Eagles threw their 200cm teenager straight in for 16 games, mostly forward with occasional ruck support, and the scoring was what you'd expect at 44 a game. Young big men take years to develop, and his 4.6 hitouts suggest the ruck apprenticeship is barely started. He's a long-term stash.
Bo Allan: Allan nearly doubled his output in his second year, from 27 to 50 across 19 games at half-back for West Coast. That's still well short of startable, with a top score of 71 all year. Hold only if your list has room for slow projects.
Daniel Annable: Three AFL games as a first-year Lion, scoring 39, 30 and a best of 53, is all there is to go on. Annable is purely a development pick at this stage. Fine as a list-clogger if your keeper slots allow it.
Brayden Fiorini: Fiorini's best years had him close to 100, including 105 in 2021 at Gold Coast, and he gave Essendon 83 in 2025. Then 2026 was gone after two games and ended with a season-ending injury. At 29, the upside is still there, but you're paying for history at this point.
Deven Robertson: Four games in 2026 at 73.5, with 52% CBA and a 104, felt like a fresh start for Robertson. He was then flagged with a season-ending injury, extending a run that has seen him play ten games in three years. Talent was never the problem; his body has been.
Elijah Tsatas: Essendon have delisted Tsatas, a stunning end for a top-five pick who managed only 22 games in four seasons. The cruel part is that 2026 finally showed the player they drafted, 79 a game with 59% of centre bounces in his six outings. If another club gives him a lifeline he's worth watching; until then he's off the board.
Jacob Hopper: The ex-Giant's 2026 stopped at 12 games, and the 66.8 he averaged was a long way below the 84 he'd delivered the previous year. He's listed with a season-ending injury and will be 30 by round 1, with 71% of centre bounces when fit. A buy-low candidate if your league hasn't already written him off.
Max Holmes: Holmes followed his 102.7 in 2025 with 97 across 20 games, mixing half-back kick-ins (43) with 45% centre bounce attendance. With DEF/MID eligibility, he is one of the most valuable keepers in the league for that reason alone. He sat out the final five rounds, so his fitness in pre-season is worth watching.
Zak Butters: The trade period's biggest fantasy story. Butters averaged 104.5 at Port off 81% of centre bounces, ranking 10th in the league, but he's now at the Western Bulldogs among some of the best midfielders in the competition. He'll still get plenty of the ball, though probably less of the centre-bounce monopoly. Minor ankle surgery in October isn't expected to affect his round 1.
Errol Gulden: The only problem with Gulden in 2026 was availability. He played 13 games, but when he played, he averaged 115 (fourth best in the league) and finished with 137, 104, 135, 147, 135. Twenty kicks a game from a 175cm midfielder is outrageous. At 24, if he's fit, he's a captain choice every week.
Darcy Cameron: Ruckmen who average 93 to 101 for three straight years don't come along often, and Cameron has done it with a lot of midfield work: 4.7 clearances and 71% CBA. He ran hot mid-season, scoring 137, 120, 122, then cooled to 101 and 88. At 31 he can't go on forever, but there's no sign of decline yet.
Oliver Florent: Carlton gave Florent the ball out of the back half (84 kick-ins) and he responded with 83.1, his best in ten seasons, playing all 25 games. After a rough first year as a Blue, he finished strongly, reaching 125 and 109 during the run home. At 28 and with DEF/MID eligibility, he offers more than most coaches realised.
Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera: He posted a 182 in round 20, then an 11 two games later ended his year with a season-ending injury. Before that he'd gone 92, 98 and 111 in successive seasons for the Saints, and in 2026 he averaged 21.5 kicks and took 66 kick-ins. A DEF/MID scorer this good is a keeper you protect at all costs.
Lachie Ash: Ash has moved from good to elite over two seasons, from 99.6 to 103 for GWS. He's ranked 13th in the league with 19 kicks and 6.5 rebound 50s a game plus 71 kick-ins for the season. That kind of damage from half-back is rare, and he's still 25. One of the safest defensive picks there is.
Josh Ward: Ward played every game for the second year in a row and nudged his average to 83, including a 122 in round 20. He's a steady inside-outside midfielder at 56% CBA, without the tagging attention the stars attract. Durable mid-tier value with a little room to grow.
Bailey Dale: Dale took 158 kick-ins in 2026, and that role has produced five straight seasons between 85 and 92. That's a floor most defenders never get near. He missed the last four rounds, and at 30 his age is the only knock.
Jy Simpkin: Simpkin's two-year peak of 95.5 back in 2021 and 2022 now looks like the high mark, with the past three seasons settling between 76 and 83. North play him across half-forward and through the middle at 36% CBA, so the scoring swings, with 126 and 59 in his final five. Handy MID/FWD flexibility on a 28-year-old.
Tom McCarthy: A late starter who made up for lost time, McCarthy took 103 kick-ins for the Eagles and turned them into an 87.9 average across all 22 games. Seventeen kicks and six rebound 50s a week is the classic half-back fantasy recipe. He's 26 and the role is his, so there's little reason to think it goes anywhere.
Lachlan McAndrew: After two games in 2023 and then nothing, McAndrew finally got the Crows' ruck job and never handed it back, playing all 24 games at 84. He attended 77% of centre bounces and topped out at 128. Rucks with a fixed role this cheap are rare, and at 26 he's only just started.
Clayton Oliver: The 2024 dip to 77 looks more and more like the outlier. Oliver has climbed back to 96 in his second year at the Giants, still winning 15 contested possessions and seven clearances a game. The days of 110-plus are probably behind him at 29, but as a high-floor midfielder he still does the job.
Billy Wilson: Wilson jumped from four games to 17 in his second year at Carlton and lifted his average by 25 points. Forty-three kick-ins and 80% disposal efficiency show the Blues trust his ball use. He's 21, scored 99 and 104 in his last five, and is a sensible defensive stash.
Caiden Cleary: Cleary has averaged under 52 in every season so far, and his 2026 broke off in the middle with a run of missed games before a 78 in the final round. He's a forward with a few midfield traits rather than a scorer. Nice to own as depth at 21, but there's not much there for fantasy yet.
Hayden Young: Shifting from half-back into the Dockers' midfield was meant to unlock Young, and he's spent 2026 halfway there at 49% of centre bounces. His 78.7 sits well short of the low 90s he managed as a defender from 2022 to 2024, and a 68% time on ground caps him. The talent is obvious; the scoring role is not settled.
Daniel Curtin: At 197cm, Curtin is an unusual kind of midfielder, and Adelaide are still working out where to play him: 22% of centre bounces, plenty of time on a wing and in defence. He nudged up from 65 to 68 in 2026. Patience is the price of owning him, and at 21 the patience could pay off.
Mason Wood: Wood's best fantasy season came at 29, when he averaged 90 in 2023 for the Saints after years of struggling at North. He's settled back into the low 70s since then and missed the last two rounds of 2026. At 33 he's useful cover at MID/FWD rather than anyone's plan.
Jack Ginnivan: Moving to Hawthorn has turned out exactly as Ginnivan hoped: three straight seasons in the 70s, now 79.4 and a 116 top score. He's a forward who goes up the ground for ball rather than relying on goals, which steadies his weekly scores. He tailed off a bit at the end and missed the final round.
Ned Long: Long's game is pressure, not polish. Collingwood's midfield-forward lays 6.5 tackles a game but goes at 62% disposal efficiency, which is why he sat at 72.7 after a career-best 77 the year before. His last five swung between 55 and 87. Steady depth, nothing more.
Sam Davidson: This was a step backwards. Davidson averaged 66 as a first-year Bulldog in 2025 and fell to 54.4 in 2026, ranking 263rd among regular players. No centre bounces and just 12 disposals a game leave him relying on goals he doesn't kick often. He's hard to justify keeping on a 10-team list.
Tyler Sonsie: Richmond have delisted Sonsie, ending a slow climb from 44.7 to 61.1 across three seasons on the wing and half-forward. He never got near the centre bounces that would have unlocked his scoring. Unless another club picks him up, he's a list spot to free up.
Tobie Travaglia: Only seven games in his second year, and a 47 average that mirrors his first. Travaglia is a neat user, at 91% disposal efficiency, but he sits on 61% time on ground and has no midfield minutes yet. At 20 he's a pure development hold, and his DEF/MID status will matter later rather than now.
Willem Duursma: The third Duursma brother to reach the AFL was thrown straight into West Coast's midfield, playing all 22 games at 72.1 as a teenager. The finish dragged, with scores of 22 and 39 in his last five, as you'd expect from a first-year body. A 30% CBA share already makes him a keeper worth sitting on.
Harry Kyle: Kyle's first season at Sydney brought 12 games and a 41.5 average, playing a quiet intercept role off half-back. His last five never got past 48. At 19 he's a long way off fantasy relevance, so he's purely a name to stash at the end of the bench.
Connor Budarick: The former Sun found real minutes at the Bulldogs in 2026, and with 37 kick-ins he pushed his average up to 66 and topped out at 114. Then a 34 in the final round followed four games out. He's a small defender with DEF/FWD flexibility, which keeps him handy as cover.
Zeke Uwland: Uwland put up 146 at some point in his debut season, which tells you what's in there. The rest of the year averaged 57.6, and his last stretch was a 32, a missed week, a 24 and then nothing. The Suns' young defender is a classic boom-or-bust youngster at 19.
Luke Pedlar: A fresh start at Port, with Pedlar saying he wants more midfield time under Josh Carr. Injuries have been the story so far: 10 games and a 47.3 average in 2026, and none of the final five rounds. If the body holds up and the midfield minutes come, he's worth something. Until then he's a punt.
Phoenix Gothard: Gothard waited until his third year on the Giants' list to debut, then kicked 1.1 goals a game across 16 matches and hit 130 once. He's carrying a season-ending injury from the end of 2026 and missed all of the final five rounds. A small forward who scores in bursts, best owned as depth.
Sam Flanders: Gold Coast's loss looked like St Kilda's gain: Flanders averaged 91.9 across 12 games as a Saint, ranked 45th. Then his year ended early, and he carries a season-ending injury into the break. He's eligible in all three lines, which makes him one of the most flexible keepers in the league once he's fit.
Sid Draper: Draper didn't play a senior game in 2026 after 10 at 29.3 as a first-year Crow. That leaves him with almost nothing to go on for fantasy purposes. At 20 he stays on the list for one reason: potential, and it'll take a breakthrough pre-season to change that.
Izak Rankine: No one finished 2026 hotter. Rankine's last five read 103, 121, 138, 164 and 129, capping a sixth straight year of improvement to 99.4. With 62% of Adelaide's centre bounces and a goal a game, he's a midfielder who scores like a forward and still has FWD eligibility. A gem for Bodega Boys.
Max Hall: Hall's second Saints season added almost 28 points to his average, from 66 to 93.9, and he wasn't just making up the numbers: 134 and 161 came in his final two games. He combines nine contested possessions with a goal a game. MID/FWD status makes him even more valuable to own.
Bailey Smith: A 117.7 average put Smith first among every regular player in the league in 2026, his second straight 115-plus season since leaving the Bulldogs. Nearly 20 kicks and 7.4 inside 50s a game is the kind of output only the very best manage. He finished with a 159. Untouchable as a keeper.
George Hewett: Carlton's tackling midfielder keeps getting better with age. Hewett was barely a fantasy name in his Sydney years and has now averaged 98.9 and 90.2 in his last two seasons. Two 130-plus scores in his last five show he still has the ceiling, though at 31 the slide could start any time.
Dayne Zorko: Turning 38 and still scoring like a premium defender, Zorko averaged 98.4 in 2026 after back-to-back 100-plus seasons. He's taking kick-ins and averaging nearly 20 kicks. He did play just 17 games and every year is a gamble at this age, but the output hasn't fallen off yet.
Noah Anderson: Five straight seasons between 98 and 104 makes Anderson about as dependable as a midfielder gets. He attended 82% of Gold Coast's centre bounces and played 85% time on ground, both huge numbers. The 2019 No.2 pick has never been a 130-a-week player, but he never leaves you short.
Lachie Whitfield: Fourteen seasons as GWS's half-back playmaker are over, and Whitfield takes his kicking to Carlton. He averaged 99.8 in 2026, helped by 120 kick-ins, the most of anyone in this group. If the Blues use him the same way, little should change; if they push him into the midfield, his DEF eligibility gets even more valuable.
Josh Dunkley: Brisbane's busiest midfielder played all 27 games but dropped from 108 to 93.9, his lowest average since 2021. Seven tackles a game keeps his floor high, and his last five were all between 86 and 113. He's 30, so this decline may be the start of the slide rather than a blip.
Tom Sparrow: Sparrow spent four seasons stuck in the 60s, then Melbourne gave him 70% of centre bounces and he jumped to 90.1. That's a role change, not luck: 5.4 clearances and over six tackles a game. The final weeks faded with a 56 and a 70, which is something to watch.
Hugo Garcia: St Kilda's young midfielder kept climbing, from 43.6 to 65.5 to 90.0, ranked 54th at 21. He ended the season with 130 and 120 in the last two rounds, after a dip into the 60s. Ten contested possessions and six clearances a game point to a real inside role for years.
Luke Parker: Who would have picked a 34-year-old to reinvent himself as a defender? Parker did exactly that at North, averaging 93.3 in 2026 with 83 kick-ins and 86% time on ground. DEF/MID eligibility makes the move even sweeter, though he's the oldest gamble on the list after Zorko.
Toby Nankervis: Nankervis's 2026 lasted just 12 games, and his average slid to 81.8 after three straight seasons in the 90s and 100s. When he played, he still attended 75% of Richmond's centre bounces and won over six clearances. At 32, durability is now the main concern.
Ollie Wines: The 2021 Brownlow medallist averaged 112 that year and has slipped to 78.1 in 2026, his lowest return since 2023. He played just 65% time on ground, which takes away much of his scoring. Still a strong clearance player at 32, but he's no longer a top midfielder for fantasy.
Blake Acres: Acres has been to three clubs and is still a solid wing scorer, averaging 82.2 in 2026 with a top score of 126. The catch is that he only played 12 games, and his 2025 slipped into the 70s. At 31, he's dependable when on the park but no longer a lock for 20 games.
Elliot Yeo: Yeo sat out 2025 entirely and returned at 33 to play 21 games at 73.0 for the Eagles. He's still getting 66% of centre bounces, which says plenty about West Coast's list as much as his ability. The scoring ceiling has dropped well below his 106 peak in 2018.
Cooper Lord: Lord lifted his average from 60 to 78 in 2026, despite playing only 11 games. His last five never dipped below 69, making him a steady player when he's in the side. At just 9% CBA, he's mostly playing on a wing or half-back for Carlton, which limits his upside for now.
Marcus Herbert: A mature-age recruit added to West Coast's list in 2026, Herbert played 10 games and peaked late with 118 and 104 before tapering to 60 and 59 in the final two rounds. Twenty-six kick-ins and 4.7 intercepts a game show he's settling into a half-back role. At 24 he's ready-made, so the job is his to lose.
Tim English: English averaged 118.7 in 2023 and has been a top ruck for years, but 2026 brought injuries and a drop to 85 across 17 games. His last game was a 54 in round 22 before he missed the final two rounds. At 29, a clean pre-season should bring him back toward his best.
Jordon Sweet: Since leaving the Bulldogs for Port, Sweet has been a solid ruck, but his average has dipped slightly each year to 78.5 in 2026. He gets 30 hitouts a game but goes at 59% disposal efficiency, which caps his scoring. He's a steady second ruck rather than a first-choice option.
Lawson Humphries: Sixty-nine kick-ins and 5.1 intercepts a game tell you what Humphries does for the Cats: he mops up and restarts. That lifted him to 81 in his third season, a career best, and he played 24 games doing it. The 124 high mark shows there's more in the role if Geelong keep handing him the ball out of the goal square.
Matthew Johnson: Tall for an inside mid at 193cm, Johnson went backwards in 2026 after improving every year since debut, landing at 65 despite playing every one of Freo's 26 games. He only attended 32% of centre bounces, and his last five swung from 45 to 108. Useful depth, but until the Dockers trust him in the middle he's a bench piece.
Darcy Wilson: Wilson finally kicked on, jumping nearly 20 points to 83 after two seasons stuck in the mid-60s. Most of it came from a wing-and-half-forward role rather than the centre square (16% CBA), so the scoring relies on running volume. Still only 21 and MID/FWD eligible, he's the kind of keeper whose price only goes one way if the minutes keep growing.
Shannon Neale: A 203cm forward who pinches the odd ruck contest, Neale is never going to be a fantasy star, but 65 a game with 2.1 goals and 4.5 hitouts is his best yet. He's played 50 of a possible 51 the last two years. Think of him as a reliable forward-line filler rather than someone who wins you a week.
Dion Prestia: Prestia has called time after a long career across Gold Coast and Richmond, finishing at 70.6 with 46% of the Tigers' centre bounces still in his last season. The 100-plus years of his prime were a while ago now. His G-Train spot comes free for 2027.
Shai Bolton: Freo got the version of Bolton they paid for in 2026: 26 games, 85.2 a game and a 138 ceiling once he was pushed into the midfield at 60% of centre bounces. That's a long way up from 69 the year before. The highlight-reel forward is now a genuine inside ball-winner too, and still has MID/FWD flexibility.
Lachlan Blakiston: A mature-age ruckman who got to the AFL at 27, Blakiston averaged 42.7 as Essendon's backup big and barely featured late in the year. Ten hitouts a game won't move the needle in fantasy. His DEF/RUC tag is the only reason he's on a list; treat him as emergency cover.
Harvey Thomas: From 46 to 52 to 73: Thomas has climbed steadily since debut and the 2026 jump was the big one. Interestingly he did it without a single centre bounce, winning his ball through 7.7 contested possessions and 3.8 tackles from a half-forward and wing role. If the Giants give him time in the middle, there's real upside left in a 21-year-old.
Darcy Wilmot: Identical 80.6 averages in 2025 and 2026, both from 27 games, make Wilmot about as steady as fantasy defenders get. Brisbane's rebounding half-back took 106 kick-ins and uses it at 83% efficiency, and he's played 107 games in four seasons. There's no big spike in his game, but you can pencil him in every week.
Joe Fonti: Fonti's 2026 was a quiet success story at GWS: 22 games and a 23-point jump to 72.6 off the back of 5.2 intercepts and 6.4 marks a game. He's not taking kick-ins, which caps his scoring for now. A cheap defender on the rise who should keep improving as he settles into the Giants' back six.
Jake Waterman: Waterman's scoring rides on how many he kicks, which is why his last five ranged from 27 to 84. He held his spot for 23 games in 2026 after an injury-limited 2025 and averaged 71.8 as the Eagles' lead-up key forward. Fine as a forward-line fill, but he's not one to trust in a must-win week.
Karl Amon: Five straight seasons in the high 80s or better made Amon one of the most dependable defenders in the competition, so 78.3 in 2026 is a noticeable dip. He still took 64 kick-ins, but he missed the final two rounds and turns 31 before round 1. Turning 31 doesn't help; the slide has started.
Keidean Coleman: Coleman has played just 15 games across the last three seasons, with only one game in each of 2024 and 2025. He got 13 in at Brisbane in 2026 at 66 a game, then moved to Essendon in the trade period looking for more opportunity. The 78 he averaged back in 2022 shows the talent; staying on the park is the whole story with him.
Zac Williams: Carlton have delisted the 32-year-old. Williams' last three seasons all sat in the low 60s, with 2026 lasting nine games before he dropped out for good, and his last 70-plus year was back in 2021 at GWS. Release him and use the spot elsewhere.
Bradley Hill: Out of nowhere, Hill posted the best year of his career at 33, jumping from 74.5 to 100.5 and ranking 17th in the league. St Kilda used him off half-back, where he took 43 kick-ins and pushed through for 17.7 kicks a game. With D/M/F eligibility, a 159 high and four of his last five over 100, ride it while it lasts.
Max Gawn: Thirty-five years old and still ranked sixth in the competition at 109.5, Gawn just keeps going. He's averaged over 100 in eight of the last eleven seasons, attends 78% of centre bounces and scores at more than a point a minute. Age is the only argument against him, and he's ignored it so far.
Jordan Dawson: Dawson has been one of fantasy's elite mids since moving from Sydney, and 2026 was his fourth season above 105 in a row. The Crows captain ranked fifth in the league at 112.9, with his 17.4 kicks and 5.7 tackles a game putting him among the most complete ball-winners going round. He's 29, so you're buying the peak years.
Tim Kelly: Kelly answered a 63.3 that looked like the start of the end. Back at 72% of the Eagles' centre bounces, he climbed to 85.5 and closed 2026 with five straight scores between 86 and 113. The window won't stay open long for a 32-year-old, but his midfield role is clearly safe.
Oliver Dempsey: Dempsey's scoring has crept up each year since he became a regular, reaching 80.4 in 2026 from Geelong's wing. He's done it without much centre-bounce time (2%), relying on run, 5.2 marks and 1.2 goals a game. After a 63 in round 20 he finished 125, 88, 105 and 114, the best stretch of his career.
Jack Macrae: Once a 120-a-game monster at the Bulldogs, Macrae managed only 12 games in his second year at St Kilda and missed the final three rounds. When he played he still scored at a point a minute, but 62% time on ground and a 77.2 average show how much his role has changed. Turning 32, he's a name more than a must-keep now.
Caleb Serong: Serong has slid gently for three years, from 108.1 in 2023 to 90.1 in 2026, even though his role hasn't changed: 73% of centre bounces and 6.8 clearances a game, still one of the hardest-working mids in the game. Playing 24 games is a plus. He's only 26, so another dip isn't a given.
Jarman Impey: Impey had the best season of his long career in 2026, averaging 86 at 31 and finishing strongly with 147 and 115 in rounds 20 and 21. Hawthorn use him as a launching half-back with 5.7 intercepts a game. He's been reliably available for four years now, which counts for a lot in a defender his age.
Shaun Mannagh: A late bloomer who got his chance at Geelong at 26, Mannagh came back a bit in 2026 to 75.9 after a terrific 87 in 2025. He's a small forward who also gets midfield time, with 2.7 clearances and 4.5 inside 50s a game, so the floor is decent. His 139 against a 65 in the last five shows how swingy he can be.
Touk Miller: The 122 he posted in 2021 is a long way back now, but Miller has settled into a 90-a-game groove for three years with very little variation. His centre-bounce share has dropped to 45%, and his last five swung from 55 to 142. A dependable MID/FWD who's past his best but still well above the pack.
Toby Greene: Greene has left GWS as a free agent and moves to Geelong, where he'll join Jeremy Cameron in the forward line. That's a concern for his fantasy output: his 85.8 in 2026 came with 33% of centre bounces, and the Cats' deep midfield probably won't need him there. At 33, expect a more forward-focused role with a lower ceiling.
Jake Bowey: Bowey has become one of the league's best fantasy defenders since taking over Melbourne's kick-ins, with 88 in 16 games to go with 6.2 rebound 50s a game. His average has gone from the low 60s to 86.4 and then 90. The catch is availability, with only 16 games in 2026 and 14 in 2024.
Luke Davies-Uniacke: Few mids attend more centre bounces than LDU's 84%, and North have built their engine room around the former number-four pick. His scoring has hovered between 88 and 97 for four years, with 90 in 2026 from 23 games. He's not quite an elite scorer, but he's durable now and still only 27.
Tom Liberatore: The Doggies' clearance machine has retired. Libba beat the age curve longer than anyone expected, with a 99.6 season at 33 in 2025, but only 11 games in 2026 told its own story. A one-club player, Tony's son and a premiership hero. His keeper spot opens up for 2027.
Jack Steele: Steele has gone down each year since his 2021 peak of 121.9, and his first year at Melbourne finished at 90.2. He's still a tackling machine at six a game with 77% centre-bounce attendance, but scores of 59 and 40 late in the year show his low end. He's still a top-tier mid, though no longer the force he was at St Kilda.
Darcy Byrne-Jones: After three years stuck in the mid-50s, Byrne-Jones jumped to 77.4 in 2026 and looked like his 2019 self at times, with a 131 high. Port gave him more of the ball out of defence, including 42 kick-ins. Whether a 31-year-old repeats it is anyone's guess, but the DEF/FWD tag gives him value.
Jayden Short: Short tried to get to Collingwood in the trade period, but the deal collapsed on deadline day and he's back at Richmond for the last year of his contract. That's actually the best result for fantasy: he stays the Tigers' main kick-in taker (91 in 2026) and half-back ball user. He averaged 87.8 with a 124 in round 20, and has a new contract to play for.
Jack Gunston: Gunston's comeback to Hawthorn has been remarkable, with 73 and 66 goals the last two years and 3.5 goals and 4.0 marks inside 50 a game in 2026. But Ben King's arrival from Gold Coast will crowd the forward line, and the 35-year-old's 71.9 average already depends on him kicking a bag. Expect more weeks like his 57s and 60s than his 129s.
Willem Drew: Drew is Port's grafter: 60% of centre bounces, 5.4 tackles and 9.3 contested possessions a game, and an average that's been in a tight 75-to-84 band for four seasons. Scores like 111 and 55 in his last five show he isn't immune to bad days. Good depth, but not a player who'll lift you into contention.
Patrick Retschko: Retschko's debut year was quietly impressive: 18 games, a 71.1 average, and scores between 66 and 82 every week in the run home. Richmond played him across half-back and the wing with 87% time on ground. For a first-year player that consistency is rare, and he's the kind of cheap keeper who can become a regular starter.
Matthew Kennedy: Kennedy's career took off late, with a 96.5 in 2025 and 88.5 in 2026 after years as a part-timer. He's now an important part of the Bulldogs' midfield, with 4.8 clearances and almost a point a minute. The one blemish is a 35 in round 21 among scores in the 90s. He should hold this level for a couple more years yet.
Hugo Hall-Kahan: Drafted in 2022, Hall-Kahan had to wait until 2026 for his debut, then averaged 72.2 in 13 games for Adelaide. He took 34 kick-ins in that time and posted scores between 59 and 77 to finish the year. If he holds the role across a full season, his DEF/MID eligibility could make him a handy keeper.
Josh Battle: Battle was on the ground for 96% of game time in his second season at Hawthorn, the highest in this group, and turned it into a career-best 76.1. He's an intercepting key back, with 6.5 intercepts a game, plus 48 kick-ins. His scoring rate is low at 0.64 points per minute, so his scoring relies on the minutes he plays.
Bailey Humphrey: Humphrey looked to have arrived with 67.8 in 2025, but he slipped back to 59.1 in 2026 and failed to crack 90 all year. He's a powerful small forward who splits his time between the forward line and the middle, but his kicking (63% efficiency) hurts his scoring. A bigger midfield role is his only path to fantasy relevance.
Connor O'Sullivan: At 198cm, O'Sullivan is a key defender who intercepts and marks well, with 6.7 intercepts and 6.6 marks a game in 2026. He's played 50 games in two years and his average lifted from 55.8 to 64.4. His low scoring rate (0.55 points per minute) means he needs a big role change to matter in fantasy, but at 21 there's time.
Patrick Lipinski: Lipinski is a utility at Collingwood who can play almost anywhere, which is both his strength and the reason his scoring never settles. His 74.8 in 2026 was his best since 2022's 80, but he missed three of the last five rounds. Useful MID/FWD depth, nothing more.
Leonardo Lombard: The Suns gave Lombard 23 games in his second year and he more than doubled his output, from 23 to 57.7. He's a half-forward who touches it 15 times and kicks the odd goal, which is fine but not yet fantasy-relevant. At 20, the hope is a midfield push; until he starts attending centre bounces, he's a stash rather than a starter.
Josh Lindsay: First-year Eagles defenders don't usually take 60 kick-ins, but Lindsay did, and it's the reason he averaged 65.9 off 15 games with a 97 at his best. Disposal efficiency of 84% says West Coast trust his kicking already. He missed two games late and came back with 44 and 38, which reads like a rookie wall rather than a warning sign.
James Peatling: Six seasons, six steps up: Peatling has climbed every year since 2021 and landed on 78.2 with 56% of Adelaide's centre bounces. The tackling (4.5 a game) gives him a decent floor. His finish was patchy, two missed games and scores of 34 and 43 among the last five, and the short-term injury he finished with is worth watching through the pre-season.
Dylan Patterson: Five games, a 31.8 average and a top score of 41 is all there is so far. Patterson is listed as a defender but the Suns used him further up, with three inside 50s a game and a goal every other week. That eligibility could become handy if his role ever matches it. Right now he's a teenager at the bottom of the bench.
Brent Daniels: Staying on the park is Daniels' problem. The 83.5 of 2024 looked like his arrival, then six games in 2025 and ten in 2026 before a season-ending injury shut him down again. When he plays he's a genuine mid-forward with 48% CBAs and a goal a game. Only 27, but the durability record makes him a cheap gamble at best.
Connor Rozee: Two games. That's all 2026 gave Port's best player before injury took the rest, and it hurts because Rozee had averaged over 100 in two of the previous three seasons. DEF/MID eligibility on a 100-point mid is gold in this format. If his body comes up for round 1, his owner is sitting on one of the best keeper assets in the league.
Liam Reidy: At 204cm and 26, Reidy is Carlton's ruck understudy and a fantasy afterthought: seven games across three seasons, none of them more than four in a year. He did attend 60% of centre bounces when he got a game, and he can score 70-plus with the ruck to himself. Useful only if the No.1 goes down.
Matt Rowell: That 182 in round 22 is the reminder: the 2019 No.1 pick has a ceiling few mids can match. Rowell's 14.2 contested possessions, 7.6 clearances and 6.9 tackles a game make him a proper inside bull, and his 98.7 ranked 26th. Six missed games cost him a 100-plus season, but at 25 there should be plenty more of them.
Chad Warner: The Swans' star has sat in the low 90s for five straight seasons now, finishing 2026 at 92.6 and ranked 43rd. Warner's forward craft (1.5 goals and 6.8 inside 50s a game) keeps him dangerous on days the midfield minutes dry up. He closed with four straight tons before a suspension ended his year, which tells you his form was the best of his season.
Josh Daicos: Ten seasons in and Daicos just posted a career-best 99.8, ranked 20th overall and elite for a defender. He gets everything from the half-back flank: 27 disposals, 5.8 marks, 52 kick-ins. Nick gets the headlines, but Josh has been the steadier fantasy option. At 28 the scoring hasn't dipped at all yet.
Sam Walsh: Healthy again. After a 2025 limited to 14 games, Walsh played 25 and averaged 99.6, almost exactly where he's lived since the 2018 No.1 pick landed at Carlton. His handball count (16.3) is among the league's highest and he took 73% of centre bounces. He scored between 82 and 116 in every one of his last five games.
Marcus Bontempelli: At 31, the Bont still ranked 14th in the competition with 102.2, his sixth straight season over 100. Pure midfielder, 78% of centre bounces, goals on top. The 58 in round 21 was a rare dip. The age is the only argument against him in a keeper league, and he hasn't given anyone evidence for it yet.
Miles Bergman: Bergman's last month told a different story to his 72.6 average: 86, 110, 92, 96 and 86 to close out a year that cost him six games. He's a big-bodied interceptor rather than a kick-in specialist (only 11 all season). The scoring mostly comes in streaks, so expect patches as well as the occasional 100.
Nick Haynes: Haynes is still going at 34 and still picking off kicks: 6.4 intercepts and 7.8 marks a game, the stats of a man who reads the play better than anyone at Carlton. His 76.5 was his best average since 2019. He ended the year on the short-term injury list, and every pre-season from here is a fitness test. A bench defender with real nous, not a long-term keeper.
Jack Ross: Ross quietly put together the best year of his career, jumping from 72.9 to 84.1 with 56% of Richmond's centre bounces. He's handball-heavy and gets dirty, averaging 10.5 contested possessions. Mid-forward eligibility makes him more flexible than his raw scoring suggests. A rebuilding Tigers side should keep handing him the inside work.
Jye Caldwell: Caldwell was a 103.6 midfielder in 2025, albeit in only 11 games. In 2026 the body didn't cooperate and nor did the scoring, which slid to 73.9 as injuries broke up his year. He missed two games late, then came back with 79, 95 and 80, a hint the talent's intact. If he's right in March, he's a buy-low; if not, the 2025 numbers start looking like an outlier.
Sam Berry: Two quiet years at the Crows, then this: 90.3 a game, 70% of centre bounces and a 156 to go with it. Berry tackles like a madman (7.0 a game) and wins it at the coalface. His last five were erratic, 41 next to 112, but the midfield role looks his to keep.
Lloyd Meek: The ruck numbers were still there in 2026 (26.1 hitouts a game, 59% of centre bounces) but Meek's average fell almost 21 points to 72.9. Two seasons in the 90s at Hawthorn made him a keeper target. Now he looks like a ruck who needs his ground ball game to come back, and at 28 his owner has to decide whether 2026 was a bad year or the new level.
James Worpel: A short-term injury and 11 games kept Worpel to a half-season at Geelong. His 79.1 sits right in his usual band. He's an old-school inside mid who tackles hard and moves it forward. The 96.6 of 2019 is long gone, but a fit Worpel getting midfield minutes in a Cats team is a reliable 75-80 option on most benches.
Rowan Marshall: Marshall's move to Geelong is the most interesting ruck story of the off-season. His 83.3 in 2026 was a long way short of the 116-117 he averaged in 2023 and 2024, and the timeshare at St Kilda is part of why. Give him the Cats' No.1 ruck job and his marking and ground-level work could bring back the old numbers, though he turns 31 this summer.
Stephen Coniglio: Coniglio's last three years have run 71.5, 60.4, 64.4, a long way from the former Giants captain who averaged 111 in 2018. He's now a half-forward at 20% CBAs, kicking the occasional goal and playing support. At 33, he holds his spot through games played (21) rather than output. Keep him on a list only as cover.
Connor Macdonald: Hawthorn's half-forward turned 2026 into a career-best 82.8 and played every game. Macdonald runs hard between the arcs and gets to 4.4 inside 50s, with a 28% midfield share that occasionally spikes. The issue is the variance: 101 one week, 38 the next. FWD-only eligibility and a 24-year-old's improvement curve make him a strong forward keeper.
Dylan Moore: Moore's averages have drifted from 93.3 in 2022 down to 76.5 over four seasons. He plays a pure forward role now, 86% game time but only 8% of centre bounces, and leans on goals and marks to score. He's durable (24 games) and not about to lose his spot at Hawthorn, but the trend is unmistakable.
Trent Rivers: Melbourne used Rivers mainly off half-back, and he scored a reasonable 76.6 there with 35 kick-ins. Now at West Coast, he's expected to get more midfield time than he could behind the Demons' stars. That's the swing factor: his 2024-25 seasons were both around 82, and a genuine on-ball role could push him past that.
Karl Worner: Worner has gone from four games a year to 27 games and a 74.9 average in two seasons. He's one of Fremantle's key interceptors, 5.7 a game, with 49 kick-ins and an 86% disposal efficiency. His 126 in round 21 came a week after a 49, which is the ride you sign up for with rebound defenders.
Josh Treacy: Treacy kicked 2.1 goals a game and took three marks inside 50, enough to make him a 74-point key forward. That's rare air for a tall forward in fantasy. His scores depend almost entirely on how many shots he gets, so expect 36s alongside 120s. For a forward line short on reliable talls, he's a reasonable structural keeper.
Jai Serong: Serong had played 9 games across three seasons before 2026; this year he played 24 and averaged 72.1. Sydney used him across half-back with some midfield time (17% CBAs), and the DEF/MID eligibility could be useful. After 39 and 45 in rounds 20 and 21 he finished with 119 and 104 in the last three weeks, the sort of close that earns a keeper spot.
Jake Soligo: Soligo's numbers went backwards for the first time. He had built steadily to 81.4 in 2025 before falling to 66.5 this year, and his centre bounce share dropped to 27%. At Adelaide he's increasingly a forward-of-centre runner, and that's not where the scoring is. Still 24, so a return to the midfield isn't out of reach, but nothing in 2026 pointed that way.
Ryan Angwin: GWS finally gave Angwin a full run, and 20 games at 62.2 is what he did with it. His job is more wing and half-back than midfield (8% CBAs), and that limits him. He opened the final month with an 84 and faded to the low 50s from there. Depth, not someone to build a list around.
Mason Redman: Four straight seasons of 84-86 made Redman one of the most consistent defenders around. 2026 broke that run, with his average dropping to 70.9 across 16 games even with 45 kick-ins. He's 29 and the kicking game (13.3 a game, 83% efficiency) hasn't gone anywhere, so a bounce back is possible.
Zach Guthrie: Guthrie is Geelong's quiet defensive glue: 25 games, 84% disposal efficiency, 4.6 intercepts a game. Fantasy-wise he's never been more than solid, and 2026 dropped him to 66.3. With only 26 kick-ins and no midfield minutes, his scoring is capped. Only useful as a reliable bench defender.
Angus Anderson: A mature-age pick for Collingwood, Anderson stepped straight into 17 games and averaged 57.5, mostly as a goal-kicking mid-forward (1.2 a game). Being older than most first-years shows in how quickly he fitted in. With 16% of centre bounces he's on the fringe of the midfield, and a move inside is what would make him worth starting.
Gryan Miers: Miers' 92.8 in 2025 made him one of the best fantasy forwards in the game. A year later he's down to 77.1, after five missed games and a flat month before an 82 in the final round. The Geelong half-forward role is the same, with almost no midfield time. He's still a quality forward option, but more 80 than 90.
Beau Addinsall: Nine games, 60.8 a game, and already a taste of the middle. Addinsall is a handball-first mid (10.2 a game) who attended 24% of centre bounces as a teenager and signed off with a 72 in the final round. A strong development hold for a Gold Coast midfield that's crowded but young.
Joe Berry: A lift from 39.6 to 53.2 across 23 games is solid progress for Port's small forward. Fantasy is a different matter: zero centre bounces and a 13 in round 20 show how low the floor sits. Unless the Power push him up the ground, he stays a bench filler.
Jaxon Artemis: Essendon blooded Artemis for six games at the back end of the year, and his 84 in round 21 was the pick of them. He averaged 49.5 off half-back with almost no kick-ins and finished the year out of the side. A slow-burn development pick for now.
Sam Banks: Banks was the surprise of 2025, a 79.5 average out of nowhere with 22 games off half-back. In 2026 that dropped to 56.8, even with 39 kick-ins, and he ended the year out of the Tigers' side. A 90 in round 20 was followed by a 12 in round 24, which sums up the year. He's 23, so there's time, but the spot has to be won back first.
Lachie Jaques: That 112 is the number to remember. Jaques managed ten games for the Dogs in his first season, averaged 60.3 as a kicking half-back and only appeared in two of the last five rounds. Seven kick-ins says the senior role isn't his yet; a regular game in 2027 would change his value quickly.
Jack Ough: Ough's 36% time on ground tells you most of his five games were cameos. The 194cm Giant still attended 36% of centre bounces and won 2.6 clearances a game in limited minutes, which is the interesting bit. Big-bodied inside mids take years, so his owner needs patience.
Jack Sinclair: Nineteen kicks a game and 72 kick-ins: Sinclair's scoring formula is the purest a defender can have, and it delivered 99.1 in 2026, his fifth straight year around the 100 mark. A season-ending injury cut him to 15 games. He's 32 now, so the recovery matters more than it would for a younger man, but the role is still his.
Nick Daicos: Only one player in the league averaged more than Daicos's 116.6 in 2026, and that was a new career high after three straight years sitting around 105 to 108. He's 24, attends 79% of Collingwood's centre bounces and still kicks it nearly 19 times a game. The R24 69 was a rare off day. As a keeper there's nobody you'd swap him for straight up.
Isaac Heeney: A Swans best and fairest, a 106 average and a 163 high, all while carrying a groin complaint for most of the year. Then the Pullman ban cut his season short. Police laid no charges and he's cleared for round 1, though the legal letters mean the off-field noise hasn't fully gone. On the field, 74% of centre bounces at 30 says Sydney still treat him as a frontline mid.
Brodie Grundy: Remember the 119 and 124 seasons at Collingwood? Those are gone, but Grundy has rebuilt himself in Sydney into a 100-a-week ruck who rarely misses. Twenty-three games, 34 hitouts and 6.2 clearances a game in 2026, with every score in his last five landing between 94 and 106. He turns 32 before the season, so the clock is ticking, yet nobody in the ruck pool has been steadier.
Zac Bailey: Seven years of averaging in the 70s or below, then 85 in 2025 and a career-best 92.3 this year. Bailey got there without a heavy centre role (31% CBAs), mostly through 14 kicks and 5.5 marks a game on a Brisbane wing and half-forward. Played all 26 games too. His MID/FWD tag is where the real value sits.
Zach Merrett: Thirteen seasons in red and black, and now Merrett is a Hawk. The scoring has barely moved in a decade: 100-plus in nine of the last eleven years, 104.1 in 2026 with 75% disposal efficiency. Hawthorn's midfield is crowded, which is the one thing that could change his numbers at 31. If he gets the same minutes, he'll score like Merrett always has.
Jai Newcombe: Pick an average between 86 and 93 and Newcombe has posted it in every full season since 2022. The 2026 version was 88.0 from 25 games, built on 7.4 clearances and 78% of Hawthorn's centre bounces. He's a contested ball winner who doesn't rack up cheap uncontested touches, which caps the ceiling (121 was his best). Durable, honest, and very hard to move up or down.
Kysaiah Pickett: Kozzy the midfielder is a real thing now. Melbourne pushed him into the centre square (75% CBAs) and his average jumped from 66 to 87 to 94 in two seasons, a stunning shift for a 171cm small forward who used to score 50s off goals and pressure. Still FWD eligible, still 25. Rank 35 in the league and pointed upwards.
Jaspa Fletcher: Fletcher's 2025 jump to 83.7 didn't stick. He slipped to 71.4 this year despite playing every one of Brisbane's 27 games and taking 62 kick-ins. The ball use is excellent (81% efficiency) but he isn't collecting enough of it to score big from half-back. The father-son Lion is only 23, so there's time, and the 109 in R20 was a reminder of what he can do.
Caleb Daniel: Moving to North after a 52.9 year at the Dogs looked like a gamble. It's paid off: 85 then 88.9, with 86 kick-ins in 2026 and 86% disposal efficiency. Daniel is a pure ball user with little contested work, so his scores live and die on Arden Street's kick-in duties. At 30 that role looks safe for now.
Archie Roberts: Three seasons in and Roberts has never averaged below 85, which is ridiculous for a defender drafted in 2023. The 94.7 this year came from 19.4 kicks, 5.6 rebound 50s and 76 kick-ins, with a 164 high. Essendon run everything through him out of defence. At 21, he's the best long-term keeper on Muzza's list after Daicos.
Tom Stewart: Stewart's best fantasy days (96 averages in 2021 and 2023) are behind him. Three years of decline have him at 77.4, ranked 121st, even with 87 kick-ins and a league-elite 7.8 intercepts. Geelong use him as the defensive general rather than a ball magnet now. He's 33 next season, and owners should value him as a reliable 75 to 80 defender, not more.
Blake Hardwick: The three-time premiership Hawk had his best scoring year since 2023, 74.4 from 25 games, thanks partly to 41 kick-ins and 90% time on ground. He's a mark-and-intercept defender with low ppm, so the scores are steady rather than exciting: nothing above 91 in the closing five rounds. Fine as a bench depth piece, not a starter you'd chase.
Rory Laird: Laird averaged 120 in 2022. Since then it's been 109, 99, 93 and now 88, one of the most predictable slides in the competition. He still marks it 6.6 times a game and his ball use is clean, but the midfield minutes have dried up and his last three scores were all in the 70s and low 80s. At 33, he's a short-term defensive filler rather than a keeper.
Jake Lloyd: The best days, 100.5 and 107 averages as Sydney's rebounding machine, now feel a long way back. Lloyd took zero centre bounces in 2026, averaged 70.7 and posted a 43 in R20. The MID/FWD eligibility hints at a changed role, playing higher up the ground at 33. Hard to see a path back to relevance in a keeper league.
Massimo D'Ambrosio: Since leaving Essendon, D'Ambrosio has been a 69 to 79 wing-half-back type for Hawthorn, landing 79.4 this year over 25 games. Zero centre bounces, decent ball use, and not a single 100 in his last five. He's 23 and MID-only, which is the awkward part: those numbers are bench-level for a midfielder.
Colby McKercher: Something has stalled for the No.2 pick of 2023. McKercher debuted at 82.3, then went 78.5 and 75.6, and his contested possession numbers are tiny (2.8 a game). The 40 kick-ins help, as does DEF/FWD eligibility. He's 21 and North clearly rate him, so a bigger midfield role would change everything, but it hasn't come yet.
Kane McAuliffe: Twenty-four games in three seasons tells you how McAuliffe's career has gone. When he plays, Richmond use him inside (46% CBAs in 2026) and the 69 average from 10 games is decent for a kid in a rebuilding side. He missed four rounds late before returning for a 75 in R24. Staying on the park is the hurdle, not talent.
Callum Wilkie: Built his way up, year after year, to a career-best 93.6 at 30 and rank 39 overall. Wilkie stays on the ground 96% of the time, takes 9.6 marks and 8.2 intercepts a game, and goes at 86% efficiency, a backline general's scoring profile. The last five (75, 94, 38, 100, 61) show the downside: when the ball doesn't come to his area, he can post a stinker.
Kade Chandler: Chandler went from three-game fringe player to four straight seasons of 23 games, with his average edging up to 69.6. He's a Melbourne pressure forward (4.6 tackles a game), so the 119 against a 47 in the same month is classic small-forward volatility. Useful as a FWD bench option, never a scorer to rely on.
Ned Moyle: A 206cm ruck who finally got a run, playing 16 games for Gold Coast after managing 13 across his first three seasons. Moyle took 73% of centre bounces and nearly 35 hitouts a game but does little around the ground, so his scores top out under 100 (98 high). He did close with 95, 88 and 71 after a slow patch. A cheap ruck backup, not a starter.
Wil Powell: Powell ended 2026 with a season-ending injury after missing the final round. The year itself was decent, 74.5 from 20 games, with a 23% centre bounce share and 28 kick-ins on top of his half-back role. That DEF/MID swing tag is his fantasy edge, but his scores have bounced around between 60 and 82 for five years. Check his fitness before round 1.
Jack Crisp: Two games shy of 300, and Crisp has averaged between 83 and 85 for four straight years, which tells you exactly what he is. Collingwood still use him as a utility (23% CBAs) and he hasn't missed more than a couple of games in a season for a decade. He's 33, and the 58 and 62 to finish suggest the end is approaching.
Isaac Quaynor: Quaynor's 71.2 was a career best by a fair margin, after a 53 in 2024 and 60 in 2025. Still, he's ranked 183rd and gets few kick-ins (seven all year), so the scoring is capped by an accountable defensive role at Collingwood. Back-to-back 47s in the run home are worth remembering. Depth only.
Peter Wright: The ex-Sun has carved out a role at Essendon as a forward-ruck mix, with 1.6 goals, 1.9 marks inside 50 and around 11 hitouts a game. That dual role produced 69.6, typical of his career, plus one 110 among three sub-60s late. He finished the season out of the side. RUC/FWD eligibility gives him some uses, but he's not a weekly starter.
Alex Neal-Bullen: A premiership Demon now in his second chapter at Adelaide, Neal-Bullen has averaged between 68 and 79 in each of the last six seasons. Zero centre bounces, three tackles and change, 0.6 goals a game. He played 23 matches in 2026. At 31 he's FWD depth, nothing more.
Archie Perkins: Perkins peaked at 67.3 in 2023 and has gone backwards since, sitting at 61 in 2026 and outside the top 240. The Bombers use him as a forward who drifts up the ground rather than a midfielder, and he hasn't cracked 95 all year. At 24 he still has a chance to find a role, but there's little fantasy reason to keep him.
Matt Roberts: Sydney's half-back flexibility hurt Roberts this year. After an 82.7 in 2025 he fell to 66.3, failed to crack 72 in his last five and never once reached 100 (92 high). He took two kick-ins all season. The DEF/MID tag and age (23) give him a chance to recover if the role changes, but the trend is going the wrong way.
Ben Keays: Keays' 107.9 in 2021 is now five years old, and it's been downhill since: 97, then three years at 77, now 64.6. A 108 in R24 came straight after a 39 and a 37, which sums up his season. A goalkicking forward (1.4 a game) with no midfield time, he's a fringe FWD option heading into his 30s.
Brayden Cook: Finally, a full season. Cook managed 30 games in his first five years at Adelaide, then played 24 in 2026 and averaged a career-best 68.2. He's 189cm and playing a mix of half-forward and wing, with 3.7 intercepts a game. Still MID/FWD, still 24. Worth a bench spot while you see if the durability holds.
Christian Moraes: A young Power forward still learning the AFL. Moraes has played 26 games over two seasons, averaging 47 and then 49.6, with just 65% time on ground in 2026. A 12 in round 21 shows how thin the margins are. He's 20, so this is a patience play, not a scoring one.
Angus Sheldrick: Sheldrick's ppm of 0.88 is midfield-level, but he was only on the ground 60% of the time, often as the sub or rotated hard. That's why his average sat at 67.5 from 20 games. He missed four rounds late, then came back for a 41 in R24. A bigger, more permanent mid role in Sydney's engine room would make him interesting at 23.
Jake Riccardi: Nine games in 2026 and none after mid-season, so Riccardi's year never got going. At his best he's a 198cm forward who pinches some ruck time (6.4 hitouts) and kicks a goal or two, good for 60 to 70. The RUC/FWD eligibility is handy, but the Giants' forward line is crowded and he's 27. Depth.
Xavier Taylor: Three games, a 24.3 average and a 36 high: Taylor's debut year was a taste rather than a role. The 191cm Demon defender is 20 and spent most of 2026 developing. Nothing about these numbers matters for fantasy yet. A stash for a coach thinking two or three seasons out.
Luke Jackson: Jackson keeps getting better. The ex-Demon averaged 104 in 2026, ranked 12th, and played all 27 of Fremantle's games, finishing with five straight scores between 97 and 122. Only 26.5 hitouts, but 11 contested possessions and 4.9 clearances a game make him a midfielder in a ruck's body. At 25 he might be the best ruck keeper in the league.
Jason Horne-Francis: The former No.1 pick has turned into the player Port paid for. A career-best 95.8 from 21 games, 5.8 clearances, 1.3 goals and 63% of centre bounces, with a pair of 100-plus scores in the closing month. He finished 2026 with a season-ending injury, so his fitness for round 1 needs checking. At 23 and MID/FWD, he's a keeper to hold.
Andrew Brayshaw: The man this team is named after has drifted back to the pack. From 113 in 2022 to 101.6 last year and now 94.2, despite a full 27 games and 77% of centre bounces. The tackling (6.0 a game) is elite, but the big possession games have thinned out (132 was his best). At 27 he's still a top-40 scorer, just not a top-ten one.
Tanner Bruhn: After not playing a game in 2025, Bruhn returned at Geelong with a career-best 81.1 from 23 games. He wasn't on the ground much (70% TOG), but a 0.91 ppm shows how much he does when he is, and 26 kick-ins help. DEF/MID eligibility makes him useful on any bench. More minutes would lift him further.
Jack Graham: Two West Coast seasons since leaving Richmond have both been interrupted: 18 games in 2025, 13 this year. When fit, the former Tiger premiership player scores in the mid 70s to low 80s, with a tackle-heavy game (6.2 a match) and some centre-bounce time. At 29, availability is the whole story.
Will Hayward: Since crossing to Carlton, Hayward had his best fantasy year by a distance, averaging 72 after almost a decade between 47 and 65. Most of it came from marking (5.7 a game, 1.2 inside 50) rather than goals. He finished the year with a short-term injury, so check his early-season availability. A FWD bench fill-in at best.
Connor Idun: Idun barely leaves the ground (99% time on ground) and goes at 87% efficiency, which says plenty about how GWS rate his reliability. His average has climbed most years, to 78.7, though his low ppm keeps him out of the top 100. Variable scores (51 to 107 in the last five) and a modest 19 kick-ins limit him. Solid defensive depth at 26.
Jordan Clark: Three seasons in a row the average has dropped, from 96.9 in 2024 to 79.7 this year, even though Clark played all 27 games and still took 77 kick-ins. The Dockers have more half-back users than they used to and his share of the ball has thinned out. At 26 he's durable and polished (83% efficiency), but the top-ten defender version of him now feels like a memory.
Callum Mills: Mills played 23 games in 2026 for the first time in years, averaging 83.7 off half-back with 71 kick-ins, and then the ACL struck. The club expects him to miss most if not all of 2027. At 29 and with the midfield minutes long gone, he's a hard player to justify a keeper spot for right now.
James Rowbottom: Tackling is Rowbottom's currency: 6.5 a game, plus a solid share of the centre bounces at the Swans. That keeps his floor respectable, but his 2026 average of 71 was his lowest since 2021, and the final month went 120, a 3, two missed games, then 100. He's a handy MID/FWD swing option and not much more than that.
Scott Pendlebury: Pendles is heading to the Gold Coast at 39 after a lifetime at Collingwood, a move nobody saw coming a few years ago. The class hasn't gone anywhere, with 0.96 points per minute and a 153 this season, but his time on ground has dropped to 68% and he missed games. Enjoy the cameo, though as a keeper he's a one-year proposition at best.
Luke Ryan: Nobody in this group takes the kick-ins like Ryan does: 108 of them in 2026, with 90% disposal efficiency on top. The catch is that the intercept marking which pushed him past 100 in 2024 has eased off, and he's averaged around 80 for two years now. At 31 he's a reliable defensive starter who doesn't miss games, just without the old upside.
Dan Houston: Houston's first year at Collingwood went badly (65.5), then 2026 brought him back to 85. Among the defenders here he's one of the better ball-users going forward, with 2.2 inside 50s a game and the odd goal, and he took 72 kick-ins. He did tail off over the closing weeks (58 in R24), so a high-80s season looks more likely than a return to the 94 he managed at Port.
Dylan Stephens: It took Stephens six years to find a home, and he seems to have found one on a wing at North, where his 85% time on ground was a career high. His average has risen two years running to 73, with a 135 in among it. He spends no time at centre bounces, though, so there's a cap on where this can go. Worth a bench spot, not a starting one.
Jeremy Cameron: The arm is the worry. Cameron needed more surgery on the forearm he broke in the grand final, it's in a splint until a 12-week review, and he's said he might have retired if he'd sat out 2026. He kicked 2.2 a game and averaged 75 after four straight seasons in the low 80s. At 33, with a broken pre-season ahead of him, don't count on him for round 1.
Bailey Williams: Williams has lifted his average every year since 2022, from 56.7 to 77.9, though most of that came in one jump in 2023. He's a mid-sized interceptor across half-back with DEF/MID eligibility, which makes him handy for filling gaps. His scores can still fall away, though, as the 43 in round 24 showed, and he missed five games, so he's depth more than a lock.
Zach Reid: After years of interrupted seasons, Reid finally played a full season at 202cm: 23 games, 87% time on ground and 41 kick-ins. His scoring hasn't caught up yet, at 59 a game with an ordinary 0.56 points per minute. He did finish with 98 and 97 in the last two rounds, which is at least a sign that a fit Reid can score.
Murphy Reid: Reid jumped from 56 to 79 in his second season, which is a big lift for a 20-year-old. He's attending a quarter of Freo's centre bounces and getting forward 4.2 times a game, so his role is growing in both directions. He's a MID/FWD and still a teenager in football terms. Keep him, because his price only goes up from here.
Neil Erasmus: Erasmus finally stayed on the park for a whole season: all 27 games, after managing only patchy seasons early in his career. Fantasy-wise it was quiet. He averaged 67 and spent only 9% of the time at centre bounces in Fremantle's crowded midfield. Talent has never been the issue. He needs a clear path into the middle before he's worth more than a bench spot.
Mitch Lewis: Twenty-four games is the headline for Lewis, comfortably the most of his career after years of broken seasons. He kicked 1.6 goals a game and averaged 64.5, the usual key-forward output with very few big scores. He's fine as a fourth forward, but even a fully fit year couldn't push him to 75.
Jacob Wehr: Port use Wehr as a running half-back who mostly kicks, and the fantasy numbers are ordinary: 52.5 for a second straight year, a top score of 74 and three kick-ins all season. He's also 28, so there's no youth upside to wait on. He's one of the first names to go when you need a list spot.
Hamish Davis: Davis is a second-year West Coast midfielder who played 21 games in a rebuilding side and lifted his average from 43 to 52.5. He hasn't had any centre-bounce work yet, and 0.56 points per minute shows how raw he still is. If you're keeping him, it's as a long-term project, so don't expect much soon.
Kyle Langford: Langford is eligible in defence, midfield and attack, and he's been everywhere for Essendon over the years. Lately that has been mostly defence, where he intercepts well (4.9 a game) but doesn't score much. He got back to 63.6 after a 2025 in which he managed only nine games, but the 86 from 2021 looks like his peak. Useful as cover, but he shouldn't be starting.
Isaac Cumming: Cumming averaged 90.6 in 2022 at GWS, which now looks like his best year by a distance. Adelaide have used him as a half-back and wing kicker, and that's produced exactly 60.5 in each of the past two seasons, with a top score of 96 in 2026. He's 28 and his role is settled, so expect more of the same.
Liam Baker: Baker lifted his average in his first season in the west, then fell away badly in 2026: 58.6, his lowest since 2020, and no score above 75 all year. The Eagles still have him in the back half, but the intercepting and clearance work that got him to 79 have dried up. He also missed the last two rounds. Of everyone on this list, he's the biggest worry.
Xavier Bamert: Bamert played ten games as a first-year Power player, mostly as a high forward, with a mark inside 50 a game and a few goals. He averaged 52 and hasn't spent time in the midfield yet. Treat him as a development pick and come back to it in a year.
Judd McVee: You can keep waiting for McVee to break out, but his average has stuck in the 50s for three straight years (52.7 in 2026). He's a smart, tidy defender (83% efficiency) who doesn't get much of the ball, and Fremantle give most of their kick-ins to Ryan and Clark, so he took only 25. At 23 there's time for a role change, but nothing in his numbers suggests one is coming.
Adam Treloar: Treloar has retired, closing the book on one of the great fantasy careers: nine seasons over 100, the last of them a 109.8 as recently as 2024. His final two years yielded just nine games, the body finally winning the argument. In a keeper league he's now a list spot to free up, and a name for the honour board.
Conor Nash: Ten games of 73 before his season ended. Before that, Nash was taking 70% of Hawthorn's centre bounces and laying 5.3 tackles a game, an inside role that suits a 198cm Irishman more than most expected. His average has held in the mid-70s since 2023. He's carrying a season-ending injury from late 2026, so keep a close eye on how his pre-season goes.
Jack Carroll: Carroll's 12 games for St Kilda in 2026 were by far the best of his career. He averaged 66.4, compared with 40 and 21 the previous two years, and his top score was 106 from the back half. He didn't play late in the year, so he still has to earn his place again. Even so, he's a cheap DEF/MID who has finally shown he can score.
Jack Ison: Ison got eight games as a teenager at Carlton, playing mostly forward. He averaged 49, kicked a few goals and missed a few more. He didn't play in the final five rounds. He's 19 and this was a first look, so how much he's worth depends on how patient you are.
Jai Culley: Culley has never had a clean run. Since his 2022 debut he has played no more than seven games in a season, and 2026 ended with a season-ending injury after seven games at 49.6. The 67.5 from his first four games is the only real sign of what he can do. He's 24, so it's hard to justify a keeper spot until he gets a proper run.
Ed Richards: Eight years into his career, Richards has become a 100-point player. His average has gone up every season since 2020, peaking at 101.4 this year, and he finished with 128 in round 24. The key is midfield time: 79% of the Dogs' centre bounces and 6.8 inside 50s a game. He looks set to stay among the league's elite midfielders.
Tim Taranto: Taranto has averaged 95 or better in three of the last four seasons, and he still wins the contested ball (12.6 a game) and attends 81% of the centre bounces at a rebuilding Richmond. The 2023 high of 112 isn't coming back unless the team improves around him. Even so, a 134 and a 133 in his last five games show he can still hit big scores, and his role at Tigerland isn't going anywhere.
Harry Sheezel: Sheezel was third in the league with 116.2, and at just 22 he's already averaged 97, 112, 109 and now 116 in four seasons. He collects the ball half-back and through the midfield, scored 173 at his best, and scores a point and a sixth every minute. He missed the final round with a season-ending injury, so check his pre-season fitness, but he's the player everyone in the league would want.
Riley Thilthorpe: Thilthorpe's role is a fantasy coach's nightmare: part key forward, part ruck (3.7 hitouts), part centre-bounce fill-in. His last five scores went 114, 57, 35, 127, 70. He went 83 in 2025, slipped to 71.6, and his efficiency is down at 61%. His good days are as good as anyone's in the forward line, but you can't plan around him.
Cam Mackenzie: Halfway through 2026 Mackenzie started to look like the midfielder Hawthorn drafted him to be. He attended 52% of the centre bounces, his average rose to 73.7, and he finished with 81, 99 and 105 in his last three games. His 0.83 points per minute shows he's scoring heavily once he's on the ground. If his game time keeps growing, so will his average.
Joel Fitzgerald: Fitzgerald was a late arrival who made an immediate impact at Melbourne. He averaged 72.9 across 11 games and attended more than half the centre bounces. He only spent 61% of game time on the ground but scored nearly a point a minute, which is the stat that stands out. More minutes in 2027 would make him a genuine bargain.
Mark Blicavs: Blicavs is 35, has played 315 games and spent his career filling whatever gap Geelong had: ruck, wing, key defender. In 2026 that meant a fair bit of ruck work (10.4 hitouts) and 61.8 a game, his lowest since 2020. MID/RUC eligibility still gives him some fantasy use, but it's on a one-year basis now.
Lachlan Cowan: Cowan's stats show slow improvement: 56 to 63 to 64 over three seasons, with 24 games played in 2026. He's a dependable kicking defender for Carlton who intercepts well, but he hardly ever takes kick-ins (4 all season), which keeps his scores down. He did end the year with a 96, and at 22 he's worth keeping on the bench, if not in the side.
Finn Callaghan: Callaghan broke out in 2025 with a 100-plus average and nearly matched it in 2026 (95.6), attending 68% of the Giants' centre bounces. He then needed ankle surgery late in the season and is aiming for full training around January, which means missing a good part of the pre-season. He's 23 and already elite, so the risk is only in the early rounds, not the long term.
Harvey Langford: So far the Demons have used Langford as a forward who pushes up the ground, averaging a goal a game but attending almost no centre bounces (1%). That role has given him 62.7 and 64.8 in two consistent seasons. The talent that made him a high pick in 2024 will only show up in fantasy terms when he gets into the midfield.
Charlie Cameron: Charlie is in his 13th season and still kicks 2.3 goals a game, and 27 games in 2026 tied his career high. He's a pure goalkicker with very little else to his game, so he's been stuck between 54 and 69 for a decade, and that won't change at 32. He's reliable for selection and nothing more as a forward option.
Riley Bice: Bice took a solid step up in his second year at the Swans, from 56.7 to 75.8, while taking 43 kick-ins and using the ball well from half-back. He's 26 now, so this looks like a player settling into the senior side rather than a youngster growing. His season finished with a suspension, so check his availability for round 1 before you lock him in.
Jacob Farrow: Farrow is a 19-year-old who averaged 72 in his debut season, which is hard to ignore. He played 21 games for Essendon across half-back, with 84% efficiency and a steady run of scores in the 60s and 70s late in the year. He has DEF/MID eligibility, so if he moves into the midfield he's one of the best keepers in this group.
Tom Atkins: Atkins is Geelong's grafter: 5.9 tackles, almost 10 contested possessions a game and 61% of the centre bounces. He fell from a career-best 88.3 in 2025 to 69.1 this year, which is what you'd expect from a player whose scoring relies on hard work rather than stats. At 31 he's a reliable bench midfielder you'd rather not have to start.
Mattaes Phillipou: After a lost 2025 (seven games at 35.9), Phillipou got back to 67.8 and spent 30% of the time at the Saints' centre bounces. He finished the year with a 94, his best since he showed what he could do as a teenager, and MID/FWD eligibility helps him. He's 22, so there's still time for him to develop, but he's stalled for two years.
Daniel Rioli: Rioli peaked at 83.5 in his last year at Richmond, but two seasons at the Suns have parked him around 70. The 30 kick-ins across 2026 aren't enough to lift a game built on 10 kicks and tidy 83% efficiency, and his final month barely cracked 70. Turning 29, he's a reliable bench body rather than someone who wins you a week.
Nicholas Madden: Only nine games in, but the Giants' 204cm big man is already taking 23 hitouts a game and attending 63% of centre bounces when he plays. The 111 he dropped shows what's possible; the 36 shows what happens when he's out of the ruck. At 22 he's a slow-burn ruck stash, and you keep him if you've got the list spot to wait.
Kieren Briggs: Back-to-back 92s at GWS in 2023 and 2024 had Briggs in the top-ruck conversation, then the numbers slipped to the low 70s for two years. Richmond is the reset: a rebuilding club that should hand him the number one job outright. The 134 he hit in 2026 says the ceiling is still in there.
Harry Himmelberg: Himmelberg's intercept game carried him to 80-plus twice since moving to defence, but 2026 was his worst year since the switch at 64.1. Six intercepts a game and 37 kick-ins should score better than that, and they did in 2024. He turns 30 before the season and never missed a week in 2026, so durability isn't the problem; the output is.
Sam De Koning: A 204cm key defender who rucks a bit isn't built for fantasy, and four straight seasons between 47 and 57 confirm it. De Koning's value to Geelong is spoiling and holding down the best forward, not racking up possessions. Missing three of the last five rounds didn't help, and his best score all year was 90. Strictly a depth pick in this league.
Caleb Windsor: Three seasons in and Windsor's average hasn't moved off the high 50s. He's a run-and-carry wingman for Melbourne who spends a third of centre bounces in the middle, but 6.7 handballs and modest tackle numbers keep his scores flat. The DEF/MID tag is useful, and at 21 there's time, yet nothing in 2026 suggested a jump is imminent.
Taj Hotton: Ten games at Richmond produced a 48.6 average and a high score of just 69, which tells you everything about where Hotton sits right now. He gets his hands on it in close, with seven contested possessions a game, but kicks only four times. He's 20 and the Tigers will keep playing him, so he's a hold for the long view only.
Josh Rachele: Rachele finally got a full season in, playing 25 games, yet his average landed at 69, below what he managed in his second year. He's a goal-kicking small forward who chips in 1.7 a game, and the 124 shows his best days are fun. The last five rounds read 54, 48, 30, 62, 46, which is a frustrating way to finish for a coach starting him.
Oliver Greeves: Four games in his debut season for Hawthorn, with an 18 and a 65 to finish, isn't much to go on.
