Greeves is a 191cm midfielder who played only 55% of game time and hardly went near the centre bounces. He's a developmental keeper, worth a spot only if your list has the patience for a two or three-year project.
Christian Salem: Salem was a 93-average weapon in 2025, the type of rebounding half-back who lives on kick-ins and long kicks. Then 2026 collapsed: nine games, 58.1, and a run of 42, 31, 51, 41 before he dropped out of the side. At 31 that drop is alarming, and you'd want to see him back in Melbourne's back six before trusting him again.
Lachlan Carmichael: Two games, scores of 33 and 26, and a debut season that was really just a taste. Carmichael is a 19-year-old Bulldogs defender with DEF/MID eligibility and not much else to judge yet. Holding him costs you a list spot that could be doing more, though teenagers drafted in 2025 rarely show their hand in year one.
Jordan Ridley: When fit, Ridley is a classy intercepting half-back who averaged 88 across nine games in 2024. The last three years have been hard: 26 games total, and 2026 finished with a score of 3 in his last appearance and a season-ending injury. Geelong gives him a fresh start and a system that's been kind to his type, so he's a cheap gamble if the body cooperates.
Jack Bowes: Bowes heads to Essendon after a stint at Geelong that peaked with 77.5 in 2024 and then fell away. Only nine games in 2026 at 69.9, and he didn't play any of the last five rounds. He's a utility who can play half-back, wing or inside, and at the Bombers he should get more midfield minutes than he saw at the Cats, where he attended just 7% of bounces.
James Leake: Five games for the Giants in 2026 before a season-ending injury brought it to a close. Leake is a 21-year-old tall defender with DEF/FWD eligibility and 80% kicking efficiency, but a 49.6 average says he's still finding his place in the side. Keep him only if you have a spot for a long-term flyer.
Josh Smillie: Two years on Richmond's list and still no senior game, with 2026 ending under a season-ending injury. He's a big-bodied 195cm midfielder, exactly the type of inside prospect the Tigers' rebuild leans on. Zero AFL games means zero data, so his keeper value is purely about patience and draft pedigree.
Nic Martin: In 2024 Martin averaged 107.2 as a MID/FWD, one of the best returns at that position in the competition. He followed it with 97.4 across 16 games in 2025, then didn't play at all in 2026 and finishes the year with a season-ending injury. If he's right, he's a top-tier forward at 25. If you're holding him, this pre-season matters more than any.
Sam Marshall: Marshall got just two games at Brisbane in 2026, and the move to St Kilda is really about finding a place he can play every week. He averaged 41 in his first season and 56 in those two outings. At 21 the Saints offer more opportunity, but there's nothing here yet to treat him as more than a rookie-priced punt.
Will Ashcroft: Few young midfielders climb this smoothly: 82.9, 86.6, 98.3 and now 105.6, good for eighth in the competition. The Norm Smith Medallist attends 65% of centre bounces and hits 17 kicks a game, and he played all 27 matches in 2026. His last five scores never dropped below 99, which says a lot. At 22 he might be the keeper the whole league wants.
Jase Burgoyne: The jump everybody waited for came in 2026: Burgoyne went from 74 to 90.4 and finished 47th in the league. He's become Port's damaging rebounder with midfield minutes on top, which explains the 137 and 140 in his final five. DEF/MID eligibility makes him extra flexible, and at 23 he's one of the best value keepers anywhere.
Joe Richards: Richards came out of nowhere to average 81.7 in 2026, up from 65.3. He's a small forward who now gets a quarter of the centre bounces and tackles hard, 4.5 a game. He finished with 101 and 103 before missing the last three rounds. FWD eligibility makes that midfield time gold, and Port seem happy to keep using him there.
Will Setterfield: Nobody doubts Setterfield's scoring when he's out there: 92, 99, 95.9 and 89.9 over the last four years, with a 141 in the final month of 2026. The issue is that he's played 38 games across those four seasons. The ceiling is elite, but he hasn't played more than 13 games in a year since 2020, and drafting him means planning around his absences.
Nick Blakey: Blakey was Sydney's kick-in specialist, taking 119 of them in 2026 on the way to a career-best 86. He leaves the Swans for North Melbourne and a club that should hand him the ball at half-back in a big way. His 2026 finished with a suspension, but the role at North could take him even higher.
Jagga Smith: After his first year at Carlton was lost entirely, Smith played every week in 2026 and averaged 82 with a 114 in round 24. Fourteen handballs a game and 56% of centre bounces is a real midfield role for a first-year player. The MID/FWD tag is a bonus, and his ceiling is the reason Carlton picked him so high.
Daniel McStay: McStay spent most of his career hovering around the 50s, but 2026 was his best season at 65 a game, and the finish was outstanding: 90, 118, 115 before a 79 and a 29. He kicked two goals a game and pinch-hit in the ruck at Collingwood. At 31 he's an occasional forward starter rather than a keeper building block.
Bailey J. Williams: A career-high 83.3 turned Williams from part-timer into West Coast's main ruck in 2026. He attends 83% of centre bounces and takes 30 hitouts a game, a full-time ruck load. The RUC/FWD tag makes him handy, and his last five never fell under 70, which is about as steady as rucks get.
Andrew McGrath: McGrath's fantasy floor used to be dependable, eight straight years in the 70s and 80s. That trend has turned: 84.2 in 2024, 74.9 in 2025, and 70.5 now. He's still Essendon's composed half-back with 82% efficiency, and the 120 in round 24 was a timely reminder. At 28, he's a solid D4 or D5, not a scorer you build around.
Levi Ashcroft: Will's younger brother has played every game in two seasons, 54 straight, and nudged his average from 72.3 to 77.3. He attends only 10% of centre bounces, so his scoring comes from 5.7 marks and efficient ball use around the ground. Once Brisbane give him more midfield time he'll climb. At 20, he's a keeper on the way up.
Marcus Windhager: Windhager made his name as a tagger at St Kilda, but he's now a running half-back and midfielder who has averaged 82 and 83.5 the last two years. He played all 23 games in 2026, and his last five never dipped below 58. The DEF/MID tag makes him a handy swing option for any list. He's 23 and his trajectory is good.
Ben Ainsworth: After sliding to 56.6 in 2025, Ainsworth bounced back to 74.4 at Carlton, his best since 2022. He's a lively small forward who kicks a goal or more a game and played all 25 matches. The 105 in the last round was his highlight, though he scored under 70 in two of those five weeks. At 29 he's a cheap forward stopgap.
Lachie Schultz: Schultz is the tackling small forward Collingwood rely on for pressure, 4.6 tackles a game, and his fantasy output has bounced between 62 and 78 for four years. He kicked 1.1 goals a game and finished the season at 73, but he missed the final round. A forward bench option at best.
Cam Rayner: Rayner hasn't missed a game in three seasons, 81 straight, and averaged between 67.8 and 68.9 across all three. That's remarkable consistency, and it also tells you exactly where the ceiling is. The former number one pick still has bursts like the 114, but he's a reliable forward fill-in for Brisbane rather than a match-winner in fantasy.
James Sicily: Hawthorn's captain is 32 now and still taking 7.1 marks and 8.4 intercepts a game from the back half. His 83 average in 2026 was a lift on 2025's 77.7, and he played 24 games. The 104.5 of 2023 is probably gone, but he remains one of the league's most dependable defenders, with 49 kick-ins on top.
Sam Durham: Durham's 2024 breakout to 83 has settled into the mid-70s, and 2026 ended with a season-ending injury after he'd played 20 games at 75.2. He's an inside midfielder at Essendon, attending 55% of centre bounces with nine contested possessions a game. The MID/FWD eligibility makes him useful, but he needs a clean pre-season to recapture that 2024 level.
Milan Murdock: Murdock was a mature-age pick-up by West Coast and played 20 games in his first season, averaging 69.8. He signed off with a 102 in round 24, but the four weeks before it were all in the 50s and 60s. He's a tackling forward with MID/FWD eligibility, turning 26, so this is close to the player he'll be.
Aaron Naughton: Naughton is one of the best contested marks in the game, 2.7 marks inside 50 and 2.1 goals a game, but those big-forward numbers rarely translate to big scores. His average has never cracked 72, and 64.3 in 2026 was a step back. He can hit 123 on a good day, but he's a rotation forward who leaves you frustrated more weeks than not.
Sam Draper: Draper played 26 games for Brisbane in his first year at the Lions, but his average fell to 61.7, his worst since 2022. He isn't an elite hitout man, 21.2 a game, with only 54% disposal efficiency. RUC/FWD eligibility gives him some flexibility, but he's an R2 at best.
Harry Rowston: Rowston made 12 appearances for GWS and his average climbed to 62.3, his best so far. His scores were remarkably steady, all between 46 and 69 in the last five weeks, which is a fairly low range. He's 22, picks up some midfield minutes (37% of centre bounces), but needs a bigger role to be relevant.
Tom De Koning: Back-to-back seasons in the mid-80s at Carlton made De Koning one of the better rucks around, which is why his first year at St Kilda landing at 64.3 is such a puzzle. Only 18.2 hitouts a game and a pair of scores in the low 40s late in the year tell the story. He finished the year out of the side and goes into the summer with plenty to prove.
Christian Petracca: Petracca averaged 111.5 back in 2021 and was a fantasy giant for years. His first season at Gold Coast landed at 81.2, his lowest since 2019, and his final four scores were all 75 or below. He still attended 57% of centre bounces and won 11 contested possessions a game, so the role is there. At 31, with a season-ending injury, it's hard to tell how much is left.
Tom McCartin: McCartin spent eight seasons as a defensive key back who barely scored, and then 2026 happened: 68.5, by a distance his best year. Eight intercepts and 6.5 marks a game, with 92% time on ground, pushed him into fantasy relevance. Last five scores include a 30 and a 31 though, so the volatility is real. At 27 it's a role change worth having on your bench, not a fluke you should chase.
Dante Visentini: Port gave Visentini his longest run yet, 15 games, and his average went backwards to 42.7. Twelve hitouts and 26% of centre bounces at 71% game time is backup-ruck work, and a ranking of 279th tells you how far off fantasy relevance that is. He's 202cm and only 24, so he stays on the list as a development stash, nothing more.
Xavier Lindsay: Seven games and a 13 in his last outing sums up a stop-start second year. When he played, Lindsay did show a useful pattern: almost ten kicks, nearly four rebound 50s and 22 kick-ins in a handful of matches. That half-back role, with DEF/MID eligibility attached, is the thing to watch. At 20 he's a slow-burn keeper.
Justin McInerney: Seven seasons, seven straight rises in average, from 50 through to 82.5. The 2026 jump came with 56% of centre bounces, and his 122 shows there's a big score in him when the Swans let him go inside. The catch is that he missed the final five rounds and played only 14 games. MID/FWD status makes him handy depth.
Kane Farrell: Farrell posted a career-best 81.9 off 16 kicks and 48 kick-ins in 13 games before his season ended early. He's turned into one of Port's most dependable rebounders and a reliable defensive scorer since 2024. Hand him a clean pre-season and the high-70s-to-low-80s floor should be back, with the odd 120 in it.
Sam Darcy: Luke Darcy's kid looked like a fantasy weapon in 2025 at 82 a game, which is a rare number for a 208cm key forward. Then 2026 gave him just six games at 63.5 before his year ended. Two goals a game and a bit of ruck relief give him a ceiling no other tall forward offers, but his body has to hold up first.
Tom Green: The ACL took all of 2026 from him, a year after he'd averaged 97.5 and two seasons removed from a 108.7. Green has since signed a two-year extension at GWS, rehab is reportedly on track, and round 1 against Adelaide is the target. Hold him at whatever it costs: a healthy Green is a top-ten midfielder.
John Noble: Collingwood's loss has been Gold Coast's gain. Noble cracked 100 in 2026, 18th in the league, off almost 18 kicks, 5.5 rebound 50s and 58 kick-ins. Two 150-plus scores in his last five show the ceiling, while a 61 shows the occasional dip. He's 29 now, but defenders built on kicking age well.
Hugh McCluggage: Something went wrong for McCluggage in 2026. He'd averaged 98 and 101 the two years before, then dropped to 74.5 with only 40% of centre bounces and patchy time on ground. He finished on a 115 before missing the last three rounds. Too good to write off on one down year, but his price should reflect it.
Dyson Sharp: Few first-year mids finish the way Sharp did: 102, 91, 102, 95 and 76 in his last five games. A 70.9 average across 15 games undersells him, since the back half of his season was much better than the start. He's already attending 37% of centre bounces at 19, and keepers like him tend to pay off for years.
Lachie Neale: Two Brownlows, a career average hovering near 100, and 27 games in 2026 at 98.9. He's 33 now and heading to Collingwood, where the midfield is crowded and his 78% centre-bounce share isn't guaranteed. A 159 this year proves he can still go huge. In a keeper league he's a win-now piece for one or two more seasons.
Patrick Cripps: Cripps is still at 80% of Carlton's centre bounces and still winning 14 contested possessions a game. His 90.3 was nowhere near his Brownlow years, but 25 games and a last five that hardly dipped below 95 show he's healthy and needed. At 31 and with a low disposal efficiency, his ceiling has come down. His floor hasn't moved much.
Tristan Xerri: Since breaking out in 2024, Xerri has gone 114.5, 105, then 96.5. The slide is real, but he was still the 29th-ranked scorer, still took 21 hitouts and won 14 contested possessions a game for the Roos. Ruckmen who can also tackle at almost six a game are rare. He's still a ruck you can build a side around.
Wayne Milera: Finally, a full season of what Milera always threatened. He averaged 93 off 79 kick-ins (one of the bigger loads in the comp), 5.8 intercepts and 84% disposal efficiency, after years of injury and scoring in the 70s. He missed a three-week block late and came back with 111. At 29 there's no long runway, but the role suits fantasy perfectly.
Sam Swadling: A first-year Magpie who strung together 110 and 104 late before a 50 and then two missed games. Swadling played on the wing with no centre bounces, using his 10 kicks and 3.4 intercepts to score at 70 across nine matches. Promising for a rookie. Whether Collingwood's midfield turnover opens a bigger role is the thing to track.
Adam Cerra: Cerra's career goes up and down by year: 94.9, then 72.5, then 95.1, and now back down to 83. The 2026 version spent more time at half-back, which is where the 25 kick-ins came from, with only 18% of centre bounces. He was steady late, from 85 to 91. If Carlton push him back into the middle, the mid-90s return.
Jordan De Goey: His 22 games in 2026 were the most he'd played since 2023, and the 83.5 that came with them was a big rebound from 57.5. De Goey split time between the centre (49% of bounces) and a forward pocket, and scores like 117 and 127 show he can still go big. He turns 30 this summer and has a long injury history. Enjoy him while he's fit.
Logan Morris: Brisbane's young forward has improved his average by 14 points two years running, reaching 70.5 in 2026 off 2.8 goals and three marks inside 50 a game. He didn't miss a match in 26 games. The 122 and the 33 within three weeks of each other show how goal-dependent his scoring is. That's normal for a 21-year-old key forward.
Jarrod Berry: Two steady seasons in the mid-80s came to an end in 2026, with Berry slipping to 75 and finishing on 61 and 53. He had almost no centre-bounce work (2%), spending most of his time on the wing and drifting back to help the defence. He's 29 and durable, a useful bench player who's unlikely to score heavily again.
Marc Pittonet: For once Pittonet stayed on the park, playing 22 games, the most in his career, and his average stayed at 70. He did the heavy ruck work, taking 23.7 hitouts and attending 76% of centre bounces, but he doesn't get much of the ball around the ground and topped out at 104. He's a reliable second ruck, not someone to start every week.
Oliver Hollands: Hollands spends 85% of the game on the ground, more than nearly anyone, and the 23-year-old's averages show steady growth from 55.9 to 76. Then his 2026 stopped after 14 games, with a 72 the last thing he played. Playing mostly at half-back with DEF/MID status adds flexibility. He keeps improving, just not dramatically.
Ryley Sanders: The Bulldogs' 2023 top-ten pick lifted 13 points to 79, playing 23 games with 14 handballs and 3.5 clearances a game. His scoring was flat late, with every one of his last five between 63 and 84. He's shown no top-end yet beyond a 109. With 35% of centre bounces at 22, he's only going to get more midfield time.
Paul Curtis: Curtis is a forward-pocket scorer who combines goals with pressure: 1.9 goals and 3.6 tackles a game. His 2025 jump to 71 held at 68.7 in 2026, and the last five ran anywhere from 40 to 103. He'd need more midfield minutes to rise above that. For now he's a FWD-line filler who rarely hurts you and rarely wins you a week.
Nate Caddy: Caddy is built and paid as a key forward, and that shows in his fantasy output: 2.1 goals a game, 55% disposal efficiency and an average just under 60 after three seasons. He played 22 games at 87% time on ground, so availability isn't a problem. He opened the last five with 100 and then couldn't get back near it. He's a slow developer.
Liam Duggan: Since peaking at 96.3 in 2023, the Eagles' veteran defender's numbers have fallen off: 88.7, 79, and now 75.2. His late-season scores were remarkably consistent, four straight in the low 60s, which in fantasy terms is consistent in the wrong direction. He still gets kick-ins and intercepts, but at 30 he's a depth defender now.
Ed Langdon: Langdon barely left the field, at 90% time on ground, and his DEF/MID/FWD tag makes him one of the most flexible players to own. The scoring hasn't matched it: 74.2 for the second straight year, with a 38 and a 47 in his last five. The former Docker is 31 and his scores have settled in the mid-70s. He's useful mainly as a utility bench player.
Logan Evans: Port's young defender bounced back from a quiet 2025 with 71.4 in 2026, collecting 47 kick-ins and 4.4 intercepts at 81% disposal efficiency. A season-ending injury after 19 games, finishing on 56, slightly dulls it. Turning 21 and already getting senior responsibility, he's the type of defender whose scoring rises once the club trusts him with the ball.
Joel Jeffrey: Jeffrey's first full season in Gold Coast's defence brought 75.6 in 2025. That fell to 70.7 in 2026, with 33 and 42 among his last five. The 83% disposal efficiency and 30 kick-ins are solid, but Noble has the bigger defensive role at the Suns. He's a DEF bench option who occasionally scores well.
Sam Lalor: The top pick from the 2024 draft has played 23 games in two years, and both seasons ended early. When available, Lalor attends almost half of Richmond's centre bounces and averaged 63.2 in 2026, a solid step from 54. A 17 among his last few games shows how raw he still is. He's 20, so his long-term keeper value outweighs any 2027 return.
Mason Cox: The American is 35 and still going, now at Fremantle as a backup ruck. He averaged 44 off 53% time on ground in 2026 and peaked at 70. He's on a roster for his RUC/FWD tag and emergency cover, not for scoring. Any keeper league coach should be using this spot on someone with more of a future.
Sullivan Robey: Robey had a promising debut season with Essendon, playing 15 games at 62 with 3.7 clearances and 33% of centre bounces, before a season-ending injury kept him out of the final month. At 192cm and only 19, he has the frame to be an inside mid. Rookies like him take time; hold him and see what the second-year jump looks like.
Angus Clarke: After a 62.2 debut season showed some promise, Clarke's 2026 shrank to six games at 53.8, with a 26 and a 37 in his last few matches. He played mostly as a forward in 2026 despite his DEF/MID status, which didn't help his scoring. He's 20 and still clearly a project for Essendon. A spot on the bench is the best use of him for now.
Sam Grlj: A first-year Tiger who played 21 games, which tells you Richmond rate him. Grlj averaged 55.1 mostly on the wing and half-back, with a 90 his highest score, and his last five barely moved between 33 and 56. He'll need a bigger role to become a fantasy option. Treat him as a long-term development pick with DEF/MID flexibility.
Luke Trainor: Trainor is a tall Richmond defender who reads the play well, averaging 3.2 intercepts and 3.5 rebound 50s, but his scores have stalled at 55 and 54 across his first two seasons. He has occasional good games, including a 102, but low-30s scores show up too often. At 195cm and 20, he's mainly a long-term hold rather than a bench option.
Ben Camporeale: Delisted by Carlton without a senior game. Scott's son came in as a father-son pick, but two seasons on the list never produced a debut, so there's nothing to hold onto in fantasy terms. Treat his spot as an open slot for the draft.
Jack Viney: One game in 2026, a 55 in limited minutes, after he'd averaged 88 the year before. The ex-Demons skipper has now joined West Coast, where his contested work could earn him plenty of midfield time. At 32 and coming off a lost season, though, he's a depth option rather than a starter. A big comeback year would be a bonus.
Kaleb Smith: Richmond have delisted Smith after three years, eight games at 42.4 in 2025 the best of his output and nothing at all in 2026. There's no fantasy case to keep him, so his list spot is a free swing at the draft.
Tom Powell: Powell's 2024 and 2025 seasons showed real improvement, from 78.7 to 86.9, built on a regular role between the wing and half-forward. 2026 gave him just eight games at 71.2, and he didn't feature after that. His MID/FWD status adds value if he gets back in, and the earlier progress suggests the mid-80s are there with a full year.
Tyan Prindable: A 2025 draftee who hasn't played a senior game yet for Collingwood. With no numbers to evaluate, his place on a list is purely speculative. A debut in 2027 would at least show what role the Pies have in mind for him. Until then, he's a low-priority spot to free up if a better rookie comes along.
Xavier Duursma: The ex-Power wingman gave Essendon 81.8 and 78.8 in his first two years there, then slid to 65.2 in 2026 before a season-ending injury cost him the run home. His 80% disposal efficiency is good, but zero centre bounces and few clearances cap what he can score. He's 26, often injured and stuck somewhere between the high 60s and high 70s.
